data.content_ref: inline:The target's mechanism asserts that elimination leaves a single 'last man standing' whose preference is merely procedural ('We act on the last man standing simply because the others are dead'), but the target's OWN countercondition concedes that if the set of possible theories is infinite, 'elimination never leaves a best candidate.' These two commitments are mutually inconsistent. Under the admitted countercondition, elimination at any finite stage leaves MULTIPLE non-eliminated theories (underdetermination is the normal case, not an edge case). When more than one theory survives, the target can no longer derive a unique preference from elimination alone; it must introduce an additional selection criterion among survivors. That extra criterion is precisely an inductive or quasi-inductive step — it must appeal to the degree or kind of past survival as a basis for future preference — which is the very 'smuggling' charge the target claims to have dissolved. So the argument only works in the degenerate case of a single survivor, which the target itself admits is not guaranteed. The biological analogy also cuts against the target: evolution does not 'prefer' survivors in a normative or truth-conducive sense, and surviving lineages routinely go extinct later; mere non-elimination to date does not, by itself, justify acting on one theory over its still-standing rivals.
